titleStmt.title: Genetic Approach for Real-Time Scheduling on Multiprocessor Systems

analytic.title: Genetic Approach for Real-Time Scheduling on Multiprocessor Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time scheduling of concurrent tasks on multiprocessor systems is a complex job, which implies finding a feasible solution in a multi-dimensional space. In order to reduce the search time we propose a genetic approach for two important aspects of the scheduling problem: task allocation and deadline assignment. We combine a genetic search engine with a simulation tool in order to find a scheduling strategy that assures the fulfillment of all time restrictions. Our system model includes a wide range of multiprocessor systems, from parallel systems to network-based distributed ones and from independent task sets to chains of tasks organized as concurrent transactions. The paper gives details regarding the adaptation of genetic operators for the scheduling problem.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: In case of real-time systems, the designer must find a scheduling strategy, which assures that all tasks of an application are finished before their deadlines. In the case of single processor systems the real-time schedulability problem was properly studied and a significant number of theoretical results [1] were obtained. There are optimal scheduling algorithms that can find a feasible task execution plan (if such a solution exists) and there are analytical methods for evaluating the worst-case execution time (WCET) for a given set of tasks with known time parameters.

In case of multiprocessor systems, the schedulability problem is much more complex [2]; there are no proven optimal scheduling algorithms (except for some particular cases) and an analytical evaluation of the tasks' WCET is in many cases hard to find [3]. However, as multiprocessor systems (e.g. multi-core processors, GPUs, distributed systems, etc.) are becoming the typical computing platform for today's applications, new and pragmatic solutions must be found even in the case of much more restrictive real-time systems.

In this context, we combined two techniques, genetic search and simulation in order to find feasible solutions for real-time application scenarios. As it will be detailed in the following chapters, the genetic engine will search for a task and processor setup that meet the real-time and dependency restrictions and the simulator performs the evaluation of the found potential results. Through an iterative process, we obtain a feasible (suboptimal) scheduling solution that performs better than other solutions found with some known heuristics.

Our contribution is regarding the adaptation of a genetic algorithm to the multiprocessor scheduling problem and specifically the definition of a fitness function that describes the real-time behavior of a given task set. Through experiments, we determined the parameters of the genetic algorithm (e.g. mutation ratio, crossover and selection strategy, population set cardinality, etc.) that performs best for the given setup.

The proposed solution may be used as a pragmatic tool for allocating tasks on a multiprocessor platform or establishing time parameters (e.g. intermediate deadlines) for tasks in order to assure the fulfillment of global time restrictions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Related work is presented in section II. In section III we describe the problem and the system model. The adaptation of the genetic algorithm to the scheduling problem is presented in section IV. The experiments are described in detail in section V. Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In most approaches, real-time scheduling on multiprocessor systems implies to issues:

• Allocation (or mapping) of tasks to processors and • Assignment of task priorities and consequently establish the order of execution Many techniques have been investigated to solve task allocation and priority assignment separately, or as a composite solution. Tasks allocation in distributed real-time systems is known to be an NP-complete problem, so an algorithm that generates an optimal solution in polynomial time, does not exist. To generate sub-optimal solutions for task allocation in polynomial time, one can use (with more or less success) heuristics such as First Fit, Best Fit, Worst Fit or Next Fit [4]. If the system workload is heavy, a feasible solution may not be found even if such a solution exists.

In the case of static task allocation and priority assignment, optimization techniques such as simulated annealing [5] or genetic algorithms [6][7] can be used. Other techniques use constraint programming [8] or combine search heuristics with Response Time Analysis [9].

It is rather difficult to make a comparison between the existing task allocation techniques, as they use different system models and schedulability analysis. For example, [4] evaluates task allocation heuristics using a periodic task model, with independent tasks, under Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Fixed Task Priority (FTP) scheduling. In [5] and in [8] the authors use periodic task models with inter-task communication and FTP scheduling, while in [9], [6] and [7] the authors use linear transaction models with end-to-end deadlines under FTP scheduling.

In our research, we consider a more general model that tries to cover a number of previously studied ones. Our model may be configured for an independent set of tasks as well as for complex transactional systems and as a parallel or distributed platform. Tasks may be allocated globally, on clusters or on individual processors. The scheduling strategy may be set for each time-critical resource (e.g. processor or network segment) individually. The experiments presented in this paper were made using the EDF scheduling strategy, but they can be extended to other strategies too. Some recent research work [6][7] uses genetic algorithms to solve transactions scheduling. Our approach differs in the way in which the fitness function is computed and the scheduling problem is modeled into chromosomes. Their approach uses a fitness function that evaluates the response time, processor load and memory usage and is computed using Response Time Analysis. Our implementation uses a simulation tool in order to determine the constitutive components of the fitness function and to evaluate the quality of the obtained solutions.

div.head: III. PROBLEM DESCRIPTION AND SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The main objective of this research is to develop a methodology for determining a feasible scheduling solution for real-time applications on multiprocessor platforms that guarantees the fulfillment of all constrains. We consider the following types of constraints:
• Real-time: jobs have to finish their execution before their deadlines. If any deadline misses are detected, the application is considered not schedulable.
• Precedence: the release and execution of a task may be conditioned by the execution of other tasks or reception of some messages; an acyclic graph defines the existing precedence conditions.
• Resource: each task can be deployed only on a sub-set of the available platform nodes, those that provide all requested capabilities.
In our model, tasks are statically allocated to processors and the scheduler assigns priorities for each task (or task instance) so that all the above constrains are met.
In this paper, we propose a genetic algorithm, which finds solutions to this scheduling problem. The system model, composed of the workload, platform and scheduling submodels is presented below.

div.head: A. Workload Model
div.p: We model an application as a set of real-time transactions. A transaction is a sequence of tasks and messages executed periodically. The precedence dependency between tasks and messages is represented through a list. A real-time transaction has the following defining elements:
• Task list (L) -a linked list that describes the dependencies between tasks and messages and determines the execution order restrictions.
• Period (T) -the repetition period of a transaction.
• Deadline (D) -the deadline of a transaction, relative to its release time.
A task in our model has the following parameters:
• Execution time (C).
• Deadline (d) -time limit relative to the release of the task.
• CPU affinity -list of processors on which the task can be executed.
The message is a special type of "task", which is handled by a network segment.

Transactions are released periodically in accordance with some external or functional requirements. A transaction instance contains task and message instances called generically jobs. The execution of a transaction starts with the execution of jobs that do not have precedence dependencies. A job is considered for scheduling only if its dependences are solved (jobs that precede it are executed).

Usually, in case of a real application, only transaction deadlines are specified. Intermediate task or message deadlines are not a-priori known. However, the scheduling algorithm requires such deadlines in order to establish the execution priorities. One of the main goals of our research is to establish a method for determining these intermediate deadlines in a way that assures the fulfillment of real-time, precedence and resource restrictions. For this purpose, we are using a genetic approach.

div.head: B. Platform and Scheduling Models
div.p: In our approach, the processing resources of a platform are modeled as a multiprocessor system P={P 1 , P 2 , … , P m } composed of processors (CPUs) and network segments. From an abstract point of view, the network segments may be assimilated with "processors" that can handle messages. Messages are scheduled for transmission on a network segment in a similar way as tasks on a processor. This model can cover a wide range of systems that span from parallel systems (without messages and network segments) to distributed ones.

We assume that each processing resource has its own scheduler. In our experiments, we used the EDF algorithm that assigns priorities to jobs according to their deadlines, so the job that has the closest deadline will have the highest priority.

The workload model has to be mapped on the platform, so that all transactions meet their deadlines. To accomplish this goal, each task and message has to be allocated to a suitable processing resource. On each processing resource (CPU or network), every task or message must get a deadline. Both, allocation and deadline assessment are solved with the genetic algorithm.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULING WITH A GENETIC APPROACH
div.p: The task allocation and deadlines assignment problems generate a multidimensional solution space, which increases with the number of processors and the number of tasks in the system. As mentioned before, finding an optimal solution is an NP-complete problem. However, sub-optimal solutions are acceptable in our case if deadlines are not exceeded. Hence, our objective is to find this type of sub-optimal scheduling solution.
We chose to use a genetic algorithm as search and optimization method, because it is well suited for problems with a large search space and multiple optimization objectives.

Genetic algorithms are inspired from biological evolution. A genetic algorithm starts with an initial set of possible solutions called population. At each iteration step, it generates a new population by means of natural selection, crossover and mutation. Each solution is evaluated with a fitness function. The fittest solutions will propagate their characteristics to later populations, generating improved new solutions.

We adapted the continuous genetic algorithm to our problem domain. Scheduling variables that must be found are task allocations to processors and task deadlines. The parameters that need to be minimized are task response times, transaction response times and the processor utilization factor (defined later).

Fig. 1 shows the pseudocode for the genetic algorithm we use. We generate new populations mostly through crossover, but also by keeping the best individuals from the previous population. After obtaining a new population, mutation is applied. The configurable variables of the genetic algorithm are population size, crossover and mutation probability factors. If at any iteration step, we observe that there is not enough genetic diversity we apply mutation with a higher rate on the population, before the creation of a new population.

div.head: A. Genetic representation of a scheduling solution
div.p: The population is composed of individuals, which represent possible solutions to the processor allocation and deadline assignment problems. Each individual (chromosome) is composed of a sequence of genes. A gene is an integer value that represents the processor on which the task (or message) is allocated, or the deadline. Each gene has its own domain of values (list of possible processors, or time intervals for deadlines). The chromosome contains pairs of genes for each task and message of a workload. The first gene of a pair corresponds to the processor (or network segment) to which the task (or message) is allocated and the second is the task's (or message's) deadline. The order of the genes is given by transactions. Fig. 2 gives an example of how the chromosome is constructed based on a system model. The example is composed of four processors, a network and two transactions (with the corresponding tasks and messages). Messages can be allocated only to the network, while tasks can be allocated to any of the four processors. For instance, the first gene shows that task t 1 is allocated to processor P 1 and its intermediate deadline is 10 time units. The next gene is for a message m 1 allocated on the network N 0 and with deadline of 5 time units.

div.head: B. Initial Population
div.p: For an efficient search, the initial population must have a large genetic variety. We generated the initial population in two steps. First, we created a number of individuals using task allocation heuristics such as First Fit or Round Robin. We also assigned the deadlines for tasks and messages choosing the smallest possible value.

In the second step, we choose a random individual from the population, copy it and apply several mutations. The obtained individual is then added to the population. In the initial population, no duplicate individuals are allowed. The second step is repeated until the specified population's size is reached.

div.head: C. Crossover
div.p: Crossover combines genes from two individuals to create two new individuals, which will have the characteristics of both parents mixed. For our scheduling problem, we use a two-point crossover operator.

The parents are selected by tournament. From two randomly selected individuals, the fittest is chosen to be one of the parents. This way we give a chance to individuals that do not have the best fitness but may have good partial solutions to propagate their genes to later generations. We allow crossover only between different individuals.

The crossover points are selected at random. We eliminate cases when the points coincide or there are at the two ends of the chromosome. As seen in Fig. 3, it is not necessary that the genes between the crossover points include both allocation and deadline genes for a task or message. Therefore, a certain task or message can inherit the allocation gene from a parent and the deadline gene from the other parent.

div.head: D. Mutation
div.p: Mutation randomly changes the value of some genes in order to find a better solution and consequently to maintain a certain degree of genetic variety. Mutation is applied on all individuals with a predefined probability factor, each time a new population is obtained.

The classic mutation operator selects a random gene from the chromosome and changes its value, with a random value from the gene's domain. We also implemented a new mutation operator, which chooses the new value from a sub-interval around the current value of the gene. The limited interval is set as a percentage of the maximum allowed interval. Better experimental results were obtained with 50% and 25% of the allowed interval. We apply this type of mutation only on populations with good average fitness, because we suppose that their genes are close to their best values and we do not want to spoil good possible solutions through mutations that radically change the gene's value.

div.head: E. The Fitness Function
div.p: The fitness function defined for our problem must express the quality of a given scheduling solution (chromosome) related with the fulfillment of time restrictions. A solution should generate a good fitness function if all the tasks (and messages) are executed (or transmitted) before their deadline. A solution is considered better if the difference between the deadline of a task (or message) and its response time is bigger. In this way, there is a safety time for each task or message and the system is more robust.

We tried to differentiate between satisfying transactions' deadlines and intermediate tasks' deadlines in the sense that transaction deadlines are much more important (because they derive from real application constrains).

Another optimizing objective was to have a rather uniform allocation of tasks over the existing resources. This would increase the system's robustness and it can increase the effectiveness of the search.
In order to express all the above optimizing goals we defined a fitness function as a weighted combination (sum) of four elementary fitness expressions. A smaller value means a better solution.

The first component f TR measures the solution's quality related with the fulfillment of transactions' deadlines. It is computed as a sum of terms, every term representing a transaction that does not meet its deadline. A term is an exponential function of the difference between the maximum response time R i and the deadline D i of a transaction. A higher positive value of the difference represents a worse solution. The goal is to have all the differences negative or equal with zero, which means that all transactions meet their deadlines.

The second component f' TR is computed in a similar way, but adds the terms for transactions that meet their deadlines. A smaller negative difference is considered a better solution. This component is weighted with a significantly smaller coefficient than the first component.

div.head: A. Tools and Methodology
div.p: For the experimental part we developed a genetic search tool, which receives as input the system model (tasks, messages, transactions, resources and scheduling strategy), translates the model into chromosomes of the initial population, runs the genetic algorithm and finally, writes a file with the results (chromosomes and corresponding fitness values).

The genetic algorithm tool is linked with a simulation tool, called RTMultiSim [10]. This tool is a discrete time-stepped simulator for real-time multiprocessor task scheduling and execution. It executes a given system model from an initial moment to a preset maximum simulation time. The simulation results are stored in a database.

At each genetic algorithm step, all individuals in the population are sent to the simulation tool, which determines the maximum response times of transactions, tasks and messages and computes the fitness value of each individual. Every chromosome is translated into a simulation model and executed for a time equal to twice the tasks' hyper-period (hyper-period = least common multiple of tasks' repetition periods). Simulation results are used to compute the fitness. Fitness values are sent back to the genetic algorithm tool, which continues the search with a new generation.

In order to explore the behavior of the proposed methodology in different scenarios, we developed an automatic task set generation tool. The tool can generate task sets with predefined cardinality and total utilization factor, insuring a random distribution of individual task utilization factors.

div.head: B. Independent Tasks Allocation
div.p: The first set of experiments was focused on finding a feasible allocation solution for a set of independent tasks with only time and resource restrictions. In this case, we were interested in the behavior of the genetic algorithm under various system loads and configurations. The experiments allowed us to adjust the genetic algorithm's parameters in order to obtain an acceptable solution in a short time. We also determined the influence of the system utilization factor over the search time of the algorithm.

The diagram in Fig. 4 shows the evolution of the fitness function for a system setup with 8 processors, 20 tasks and a relative utilization of 90%. The experiment, repeated for 5 times, show that every time the genetic algorithm can find a feasible solution in a reasonable number of generations; all the solutions under the horizontal threshold line are considered acceptable.

Fig. 5 shows the dependency between system model and the number of generations needed to obtain an acceptable solution. The experiments were performed on a scenario with 4, 6 and 8 processors, 10 and 20 tasks and relative utilization of 90%. It can be observed that the number of processors and tasks also influences the number of generations required for obtaining a good solution. It can be seen that at the same utilization factor, task sets with more tasks are easier to allocate than a task set with cardinality slightly greater than the number of processors. This phenomenon was also mentioned in [11].

div.head: C. Distributed Transaction Scheduling
div.p: The second set of experiments were performed in order to evaluate the proposed methodology in case of transactions scheduling. These experiments were much more demanding because the number of genes in the chromosomes is doubled for the same set of tasks and the scheduling process is more difficult because of the precedence conditions between tasks and messages. In these experiments, the genetic algorithm must find a good task and message deadline distribution besides a good allocation. Fig. 6 shows the evolution of the fitness function for a scenario with 12 transactions on 8 processors. It can be observed that a good solution (under the horizontal threshold) is obtained in a greater number of generations (compared with the case of independent tasks).

Experiments allowed us to adjust the parameters of the genetic algorithm for a faster generation of a good solution. In case of mutation probability the best values was 1% for shorter chromosomes (20-30 and 0.3% for longer chromosomes (more than 100 genes), and for the crossover probability of 70%. In some cases, a variable mutation ratio with a tendency of decreasing the probability in every generation had better results. The initial population was set to 60 chromosomes, as a compromise between variability and execution time; higher number of chromosomes require more simulation time.
We also observed that using intuitive heuristics for the initial population generation, instead of random generation, is a better choice for a faster search.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: The proposed methodology, which implies the use of a genetic search engine and a simulator, may be used to obtain feasible scheduling solutions for real-time applications on multiprocessor platforms. The paper presents details regarding the adaptation of a continuous genetic algorithm to the specific requirements of the real-time scheduling problem.
The main contributions of the paper are the definition of a multi-criteria fitness function and the experimental adjustment of genetic operators and parameters.
The experiments analyzed the case of a parallel system with independent task sets and a distributed system with concurrent transactions. In both cases, the proposed methodology proved to be feasible.
The tool developed based on the proposed methodology can be useful in the design and experimental validation of complex real-time applications on multiprocessor platforms.
As future work, we intend to analyze more scheduling strategies and systems with more complex network structures.
